title: Sore Throat After Drinking: Why Alcohol Hurts and What Helps
excerpt: Why your throat hurts after drinking alcohol, from dryness and reflux to snoring and shouting, why spirits burn, what actually helps, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Why does your throat hurt after drinking? Dryness, reflux, snoring, and why alcohol burns, plus what helps and when a sore throat needs a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a sore throat after drinking is common, and it's usually not a sign of anything serious. Alcohol dries out your throat, can push stomach acid up toward it, relaxes the muscles in your airway so you snore and breathe through your mouth all night, and often comes packaged with shouting over loud music, smoke, and vaping. Strong spirits also sting on the way down. Most of the time a few glasses of water, some rest for your voice, and a day or two of patience fix it. This guide walks through each cause, how to tell which one is yours, what actually helps, and the warning signs that mean you should get checked.

**The quick fixes:** drink water steadily through the morning, sip something warm (tea with honey, broth), suck on a lozenge, rest your voice, and skip the hair of the dog. If you woke up with a sour taste and a hoarse voice, reflux is a likely culprit, so avoid lying flat and eat something bland. If the soreness lasts more than about a week, gets worse, or comes with fever, swollen glands, white patches, or trouble swallowing, see a doctor.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US) if** you have trouble breathing or swallowing, swelling of your lips, tongue, or throat, hives with dizziness or faintness, drooling because you can't swallow, vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, or severe chest pain after vomiting. **Book a doctor's visit if** the sore throat lasts longer than about a week, you have a fever over 101°F (38.3°C), swollen tender glands, white patches on your tonsils, or one-sided throat pain; hoarseness lasts more than three weeks; you get a sore throat or reflux symptoms almost every time you drink; or you have a sore throat alongside shaking, sweating, or a racing heart when you go a day without drinking. That last pattern can be a sign of alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous, so say so plainly to a doctor and get checked rather than toughing it out.

## Why Does Alcohol Burn Your Throat?

That warm, sharp sting when a shot goes down is real nerve activity, not your imagination. Your mouth and throat are lined with nerve endings that carry a receptor called **TRPV1**. It's the same receptor that responds to the capsaicin in chili peppers and to genuinely hot temperatures. Its job is to warn you about heat.

Ethanol switches this receptor on. Lab research published in *Nature Neuroscience* in 2002 found that ethanol lowers the temperature at which TRPV1 fires, so that normal body temperature starts to register as "hot." That's why alcohol feels like it burns even though the drink itself is cool.

A few things make the burn stronger:

- **Higher proof.** A neat spirit around 40% alcohol activates those receptors far more than a 5% beer or a 12% wine. Overproof rum and cask-strength whiskey are rougher again.
- **Taking it fast.** Shots hit a small patch of throat with a concentrated dose all at once.
- **An already irritated throat.** If your throat is dry, raw from shouting, or inflamed from a cold, alcohol stings more, the same way lemon juice stings a paper cut.
- **Carbonation and acidity.** Fizzy mixers and citrus can add their own sharpness on top of the alcohol.

At normal drinking strengths, the burn is a sensation rather than an injury. Repeatedly drinking very strong spirits neat, though, does expose the lining of the mouth and throat to a lot of irritation over time, which is one reason long-term heavy drinking is linked to health problems in that area (more on that below).

## The Main Causes of a Sore Throat After Drinking

A sore throat the morning after usually has more than one cause at once. Here are the usual suspects, roughly in order of how often they're the problem.

### 1. Dryness and dehydration

Alcohol suppresses a hormone called vasopressin (also known as antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of it around, you urinate more than you drink, and you wake up a bit dehydrated. Your mouth and throat feel it first. Saliva helps protect and lubricate the throat lining, so a dry mouth leaves that lining more exposed and scratchy.

Add a warm, crowded bar, a few hours of talking, and a night of sleeping in a heated or air-conditioned room, and the throat can feel like sandpaper by morning.

**What it feels like:** a dry, scratchy throat and dry mouth that improve noticeably once you drink water and eat something. Often comes with thirst and a headache.

### 2. Snoring and mouth breathing

Alcohol is a sedative, and it relaxes muscles throughout your body, including the ones that hold your airway open at the back of your throat. That's why people who never snore can snore after drinking, and people who already snore get louder. Alcohol can also make sleep apnea worse in people who have it.

Snoring means the soft tissues of your throat are vibrating for hours. Mouth breathing means dry air is flowing straight over them all night, without your nose to warm and humidify it. Both are reliable ways to wake up with a sore, dry throat. Alcohol also disrupts sleep quality in the second half of the night, which is covered in our guide to [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking).

**What it feels like:** worst right after waking, especially at the back of the throat, and fades within a few hours. A partner may have mentioned the snoring.

### 3. Acid reflux reaching your throat

This one is often overlooked. Alcohol can relax the **lower esophageal sphincter**, the ring of muscle at the bottom of your food pipe that normally keeps stomach acid where it belongs. It can also increase stomach acid and irritate the stomach lining. Then you go to bed, lie flat, and gravity stops helping.

Some of that acid can travel all the way up to your throat and voice box. Doctors call this **laryngopharyngeal reflux**, and it's sometimes nicknamed "silent reflux" because it doesn't always come with classic heartburn. Late-night food, especially greasy, spicy, or acidic snacks, makes it more likely. So do wine, carbonated drinks, and large volumes of drinks in general.

**What it feels like:** a raw or burning throat, hoarse voice, a sour or bitter taste in the mouth, constant throat clearing, a cough, or a feeling of a lump in the throat. It may come with chest burning. Our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) covers the reflux side in more detail.

### 4. Shouting, singing, and talking over music

Bars, clubs, weddings, and concerts are loud. Talking over loud music for hours strains your vocal cords and the muscles around them, and alcohol makes this worse in two ways. It dries out the vocal cords, which need moisture to vibrate smoothly, and it dulls your sense of how hard you're pushing your voice. Karaoke and stadium chanting are the classic examples.

**What it feels like:** hoarseness or a croaky, weak voice, tenderness when you talk, and soreness that's more about your voice box than the back of your throat. It usually recovers with a day or two of voice rest.

### 5. Smoke, vapes, and secondhand smoke

Many people who don't smoke during the week will have a cigarette or a few hits of a vape when they drink. Even if you didn't, you may have spent time on a smoking patio or around a fire pit. Smoke and vapor are direct irritants to the throat, and the drying effect of alcohol leaves the lining less protected.

**What it feels like:** a scratchy, irritated throat, sometimes with a cough or a feeling of tightness, often worse than you'd expect from the amount you drank.

### 6. Vomiting

If you were sick during the night, stomach acid passed over your throat on the way out, sometimes more than once. That acid is harsh on tissue that isn't designed for it. Forceful retching can also strain the throat. If nausea is the bigger issue, our guide to [hangover nausea](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) explains what helps settle the stomach.

**What it feels like:** a raw, burning throat, sometimes with a sour taste and a hoarse voice. It can take a few days to settle fully.

**Important:** a small streak of blood after repeated vomiting can come from a minor tear, but vomiting more than a small amount of blood, vomit that looks like coffee grounds, black stools, or severe chest pain after vomiting needs emergency care.

### 7. A reaction to something in the drink

Some people react to ingredients in alcoholic drinks rather than to the alcohol itself. Wine and some beers contain **sulfites** and **histamine**, and some drinks contain grains, hops, yeast, fruit, or flavorings that a small number of people react to. People with the genetic flushing response (often called Asian flush) also handle alcohol's by-product acetaldehyde poorly, which can trigger histamine release.

Mild reactions can cause a stuffy nose, sneezing, flushing, an itchy throat, or a tight, scratchy feeling. If you notice the same throat symptoms every time you drink a particular type of drink, that's a useful clue. Our guides to [alcohol allergy and intolerance](/never-hungover/alcohol-allergy) and [sulfites in wine](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches) go deeper. Any swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, or trouble breathing, is an emergency.

### 8. A cold or infection that was coming anyway

Sometimes the timing is a coincidence. A night out often means lots of close contact with other people, shared glasses, and late hours, and alcohol can blunt immune responses for a while after heavy drinking. A sore throat that arrives with a runny nose, cough, body aches, or fever and keeps going for several days is more likely to be a cold or another infection than a hangover symptom.

## How to Tell Which Cause Is Yours

You can often narrow it down from a few simple questions:

| What you notice | Most likely cause |
|---|---|
| Dry, scratchy throat that eases quickly after water | Dehydration and dry mouth |
| Worst on waking, fades by midday, partner says you snored | Snoring and mouth breathing |
| Sour taste, hoarse voice, throat clearing, chest burning | Acid reflux |
| Croaky or weak voice after a loud night | Vocal strain |
| Scratchy throat and cough after a smoky night or vaping | Smoke irritation |
| Raw, burning throat after being sick | Vomiting |
| Itchy throat, stuffy nose, or flushing with one type of drink | Sensitivity to an ingredient |
| Fever, aches, swollen glands, lasts several days | A cold or other infection |

Most people will tick two or three rows. That's normal. The fixes overlap a lot.

## What Helps a Sore Throat After Drinking

None of these are dramatic, but they work for the common causes.

### Rehydrate steadily

Start with a large glass of water and keep sipping through the morning rather than chugging all at once. If you feel wiped out, a drink with electrolytes can help you rehydrate, and our [electrolyte drinks compared](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) guide covers the options. Coffee is fine in moderation, but don't let it replace water.

### Soothe the throat directly

- **Warm drinks.** Herbal tea, warm water with lemon and honey, or broth can make a raw throat feel better. Honey coats the throat and has some evidence for easing coughs. (Don't give honey to children under one.)
- **Lozenges or hard candy.** These keep saliva flowing, which keeps the throat moist.
- **Salt water gargle.** About half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of warm water, gargled and spat out a few times a day, is a long-standing home remedy that many people find soothing.
- **Cold foods.** Ice chips, an ice pop, or cold yogurt can numb the soreness a little.

### Rest your voice

If you're hoarse, talk less and don't whisper. Whispering can actually strain the vocal cords more than speaking softly. Give it a day.

### Calm the reflux

If you suspect reflux, eat something bland like toast, crackers, oatmeal, or a banana, and avoid coffee, citrus, spicy food, and greasy food until you feel better. Don't lie flat right after eating. An over-the-counter antacid can help with occasional acid symptoms; follow the label and talk to a pharmacist if you take other medicines.

### Use pain relief carefully

An over-the-counter pain reliever can take the edge off. Two cautions apply after drinking. Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin can irritate a stomach that alcohol has already irritated, so take them with food and only at the label dose. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is harder on the liver when combined with heavy drinking, so wait until the alcohol has cleared and stay well under the label maximum. Many sore throat and cold remedies already contain acetaminophen or a sedating antihistamine, so check labels before doubling up. Our guides on [cough medicine and alcohol](/never-hungover/cough-medicine-and-alcohol) and [antihistamines and alcohol](/never-hungover/antihistamines-and-alcohol) explain why some cold remedies don't mix well with drinking.

### Add moisture to the air

If dry air is part of the problem, a humidifier in the bedroom, a steamy shower, or breathing over a bowl of hot water can help the throat and nose feel less dry.

### Skip the hair of the dog

Another drink in the morning only adds more drying and irritation to a throat that's already sore, and it just delays the hangover. There is no good evidence that drinking more helps a hangover or a sore throat.

## Does Alcohol Help a Sore Throat? (The Hot Toddy Question)

Many people grew up with the idea that a hot toddy, usually whiskey with hot water, honey, and lemon, is a cold remedy. It's a comforting drink, and the warmth, honey, and steam can genuinely make a sore throat feel better for a while.

The alcohol is not the helpful part. There is no good evidence that alcohol kills the germs behind a sore throat at drinking strength, and it brings the same problems this article is about: it dries the throat, can trigger reflux, and worsens sleep at a time when your body needs rest. It can also interact with cold and flu medicines.

If you like the ritual, make it without the whiskey. Hot water, honey, lemon, and a little fresh ginger give you all the soothing parts.

## Sore Throat After Drinking Cold Drinks or Water

Some people searching this topic mean something different: a throat that hurts or feels odd right after drinking cold water or a cold drink, not alcohol. A brief sharp sensation from very cold liquid is common and usually harmless. It's simply cold-sensing nerves reacting.

If your throat hurts every time you swallow any liquid, though, that's a symptom of the throat itself being inflamed, whether from an infection, reflux, or irritation. Pain on swallowing that lasts more than a few days, or difficulty getting liquids down at all, deserves a visit to a doctor.

## Is a Sore Throat After Drinking Ever Serious?

Most of the time, no. But a few patterns are worth paying attention to.

**Signs of an allergic reaction.** Swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, a tight throat, wheezing, hives, or dizziness after drinking can mean a serious allergic reaction. Treat it as an emergency and call 911.

**Signs of an injury from vomiting.** Vomiting blood, vomit that looks like coffee grounds, black tarry stools, or severe chest or upper belly pain after heavy vomiting need urgent care.

**Signs of an infection.** Fever, swollen tender glands in the neck, white patches on the tonsils, pain mostly on one side, a muffled voice, or difficulty opening your mouth are reasons to see a doctor, since some throat infections need treatment.

**Symptoms that keep coming back.** If you get a sore throat or reflux symptoms almost every time you drink, it's worth talking to a doctor about reflux. Untreated, regular reflux can irritate the throat and esophagus over time.

**Hoarseness that lasts.** Hoarseness that lasts more than three weeks, a lump in the neck, pain when swallowing that doesn't go away, or coughing up blood should be checked by a doctor. This matters more if you drink heavily or smoke. The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies alcohol as a cause of cancers of the mouth, throat, voice box, and esophagus, and the risk is much higher when drinking and smoking are combined. A single sore throat after a night out is not a reason to worry about this. Persistent symptoms are a reason to get checked rather than wait.

**Withdrawal signals.** If you drink most days and notice shaking, sweating, anxiety, nausea, or a racing heart when you go without, that isn't a hangover. It can be alcohol withdrawal, which can become dangerous. Don't stop suddenly on your own; talk to a doctor, who can help you do it safely.

## How to Prevent a Sore Throat Next Time

You don't need to overhaul your social life to avoid waking up with a raw throat. A few small habits make a real difference:

1. **Alternate with water.** A glass of water between drinks slows your pace and limits dehydration.
2. **Go easy on neat spirits.** If shots burn, they're irritating your throat. Mixed drinks, wine, or beer at a slower pace are gentler.
3. **Eat before and during.** Food slows how quickly alcohol is absorbed and gives your stomach something to work on besides acid.
4. **Stop eating and drinking two to three hours before bed** if you're prone to reflux, and avoid greasy late-night food.
5. **Prop your head up.** Sleeping with your head slightly raised, or on your left side, can reduce reflux and snoring for some people.
6. **Protect your voice.** Step outside or into a quieter corner to talk rather than shouting over the music for hours.
7. **Avoid smoke and vapes**, including the smoking patio, if your throat is sensitive.
8. **Keep water by the bed** and drink a glass before you sleep.
9. **Notice patterns.** If one type of drink always gives you an itchy throat or stuffy nose, try something else.

Most of these overlap with general hangover prevention, which is covered in more depth in our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover). For a full list of what can go wrong the morning after, see our overview of [hangover symptoms](/never-hungover/hangover-symptoms).

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

To be straightforward about it: **there is no good evidence that DHM prevents a sore throat.** The common causes of a sore throat after drinking are dryness, reflux, snoring, voice strain, smoke, and vomiting. A supplement doesn't fix any of those. Water, pacing, food, and protecting your voice do.

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol and on general hangover symptoms. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. Some people take it as part of a broader routine on nights they drink, alongside water and food. If you want to try it, two popular options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicines, check with a pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

A sore throat after drinking is usually your throat telling you it got dry, got a bit of acid, spent the night snoring, or did too much shouting. Rehydrate, sip something warm, rest your voice, eat something bland if reflux is involved, and give it a day or two. Next time, pace yourself, alternate with water, go easier on neat spirits, and stop eating and drinking a couple of hours before bed.

See a doctor if the soreness lasts more than about a week, comes back every time you drink, or comes with fever, swollen glands, or trouble swallowing. Get emergency help for trouble breathing, swelling in your mouth or throat, or vomiting blood.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does my throat hurt after drinking alcohol?**

Usually it's a mix of things rather than one cause. Alcohol dries out the lining of your mouth and throat, it can trigger acid reflux that reaches the throat, it relaxes throat muscles so you snore or breathe through your mouth all night, and nights out often involve shouting over music, smoke, or vaping. Strong spirits can also irritate the throat directly. Most of these settle within a day or two once you rehydrate and rest your voice.

**Why does alcohol burn my throat?**

Ethanol activates the same heat-sensing nerve receptors (called TRPV1) that respond to chili peppers and hot temperatures, and lab research suggests it lowers the temperature at which those receptors fire. Higher-proof drinks hit those receptors harder, which is why a neat shot of spirits burns more than a beer. The burn is a sensation, not a burn injury, at normal drinking strengths.

**How long does a sore throat after drinking last?**

A sore throat from dryness, snoring, or shouting usually improves within 24 to 48 hours once you drink water and rest your voice. Throat irritation from reflux or vomiting can take a few days. If it lasts more than about a week, keeps getting worse, or comes with fever, swollen glands, or trouble swallowing, see a doctor, because an infection or another cause may be involved.

**Can acid reflux from alcohol cause a sore throat?**

Yes. Alcohol can relax the muscle at the bottom of the esophagus that normally keeps stomach acid down, and lying down after drinking makes it easier for acid to travel up. When acid or stomach contents reach the throat and voice box (sometimes called silent reflux), it can cause a raw throat, hoarseness, a feeling of a lump, and throat clearing the next morning, sometimes without obvious heartburn.

**Does alcohol help a sore throat, like a hot toddy?**

There is no good evidence that alcohol treats a sore throat. A hot toddy may feel soothing because of the warm liquid, honey, and lemon, but the alcohol itself can dry out and irritate the throat and worsen sleep. If you want the comfort, a warm drink with honey and lemon and no alcohol gives you the soothing part without the downsides. Honey is not suitable for children under one year old.

**Should I drink alcohol if I already have a sore throat or cold?**

It's better to skip it or keep it light. Alcohol can further dry and irritate a sore throat, worsen sleep quality when your body needs rest, and interact with cold and flu medicines, especially ones that cause drowsiness or contain acetaminophen. Check the labels of anything you're taking and ask a pharmacist if you're unsure.

**When is a sore throat after drinking an emergency?**

Call 911 or get emergency care if you have trouble breathing or swallowing, swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, hives with dizziness, drooling because you can't swallow, vomiting blood, or severe chest pain after vomiting. These signs can point to a serious allergic reaction or an injury to the esophagus and need urgent care.

**Can DHM prevent a sore throat after drinking?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents a sore throat. A sore throat after drinking mostly comes from dryness, reflux, snoring, shouting, and smoke, which a supplement doesn't address. DHM is studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and hangover symptoms, mostly in animal research with limited human data. Water, pacing, and protecting your voice matter much more for your throat.
